name: Roman Empire (Trajan)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 5.8 million km2 for 100 CE (high). Taagepera 1979 (doi:10.2307/1170959, not fetched) gives ~5.0 million km2 at the 117 CE peak (mid). The historical-basemaps world_100 polygon measures 4.62 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, low); it predates Trajan's eastern annexations of 114-117.

population.note: Seshat codes the Principate at 50-60 million for 100 CE and 55-70 million for 200 CE. Frier 2000 (Cambridge Ancient History XI, isbn:0521263352, p. 814 table 6) gives 45.5 million in 14 CE and 61.4 million in 164 CE; geometric interpolation to 117 CE gives ~56 million, used as mid. High end covers Scheidel's 59-72 million for c. 165 CE and the 70 million upper Seshat value. Everything inside the imperial border, slaves included.

urbanization.note: Hanson & Ortman 2017 (JRA 30, pp. 301-324) put ~14 million people in ~600 cities above 5,000 inhabitants, i.e. 20-25% of a 56-70 million population (high end). Mid and low allow for stricter urban definitions; Seshat codes Rome itself at 1.0-1.2 million in 100 CE.

activePersonnel.note: Holder 2003 (BICS 46, 101-145) reconstructs the army of c. 130 CE as 30 legions (165,000 infantry + 3,600 cavalry) and 381 auxiliary units (152,260 infantry + 71,468 cavalry) = 392,328, excluding ~4,000 officers. Added: Praetorian and urban cohorts (~10,000-20,000), numeri (~5,000-20,000) and the navy (30,000-46,000). Trajan in 117 also had 30 legions (II Traiana and XXX Ulpia raised, IX Hispana and XXII Deiotariana still extant). Vigiles (~7,000) excluded as paramilitary.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. No formal reserve; recalled veterans (evocati) and recently discharged veterans in colonies. 30 legions x ~150-200 survivors of 25-year service discharged per year = ~5,000-6,000 legionaries a year; a few recent year classes recallable.

supportPersonnel.note: Navy 30,000-46,000 (John Lydus gives 45,562 sailors for the fleet before Diocletian's expansion; ancient figure, late) + ~4,000 centurions and higher officers excluded from Holder's unit totals (Holder 2003, doi:10.1111/j.2041-5370.2003.tb01979.x). Mid = 40,000 navy + 4,000 officers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The standing army was ~0.8% of the population; the Republic during the Second Punic War mobilised a far larger share of its citizen body, but provincials could not be levied at that intensity. 0.04 assumes an emergency levy on the Republican pattern restricted to citizen and frontier populations.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legionary infantry 30 x ~5,500 = 165,000 + auxiliary infantry 152,260 less ~12,000 archers (Holder 2003, as tabulated for c. 130 CE) + Praetorian and urban cohorts in Rome (~10,000-20,000, estimate). Auxiliary cohorts fought as close-order armoured infantry, hence line.

quality.note: Rubric quality 1.0 row names Roman legion kit c. 100 CE as the era's best (mail/segmented armour, scutum, gladius, pilum); auxiliaries slightly lighter, so mid 0.95.

training.note: Rubric training 0.75-1.0: long-service professionals (25-year terms), drill and fortified-camp routine; auxiliaries slightly below legionaries.

count.note: Archer units (sagittarii) were about 1 in 12 auxiliary units with an official total of ~17,600 men including mounted archer alae (high); infantry share estimated at ~12,000.

quality.note: Composite bows from eastern recruiting grounds; among the era's best (0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Irregular numeri and allied light troops (e.g. Lusius Quietus' Moors in the Dacian and Parthian wars); Goldsworthy, The Complete Roman Army, chapter on the auxilia, describes the units but gives no total.

training.note: Semi-regular ethnic units; between conscript and professional.

count.note: Alae: 88 units (7 milliary) ~46,500 men, i.e. Holder's 71,468 auxiliary cavalry less ~25,000 riders of cohortes equitatae (70% of cohorts assumed equitate), + 3,600 legionary cavalry + ~1,000 equites singulares Augusti.

quality.note: Mail-armoured cavalry with spears and shields; among the era's best but not superior to Parthian cataphracts (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Mounted men of the cohortes equitatae (~25,000 under Holder's 70% assumption) + Moorish and other irregular light horse (2,000-5,000, estimate).
30 legions x 65 pieces: Vegetius (Epitoma 2.25) gives 55 carroballistae + 10 onagri per legion. Late-4th-century source applied to the 2nd century; low allows for lower 2nd-century establishments.

quality.note: Torsion artillery at its ancient peak (rubric 1.0 row: Roman kit c. 100 CE).

count.note: Educated guess: triremes and larger (one hexeres flagship at Misenum) of the two praetorian fleets. Navy 30,000-46,000 men divided between major ships (~200 men) and liburnians/river craft (~60-100 men).

quality.note: Unchallenged Mediterranean fleet, standard trireme/liburnian designs.

count.note: Educated guess: liburnians and patrol/river craft of the provincial fleets (Britannica, Germanica, Pannonica, Moesica, Pontica, Syriaca, Alexandrina); same manpower split as ships_major.

quality.note: Liburnians formed the bulk of the provincial fleets.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: trained staff system (legates, tribunes, centurionate), proven commanders (Trajan's Dacian and Parthian campaigns).

cohesion.note: Rubric 1.0 row names legionary identity; auxiliaries somewhat lower, mid 0.9.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, recent victories (Dacia 106, Parthian war 114-116), though the 115-117 Jewish diaspora revolt and eastern unrest weighed on 117.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (300 BCE: iron weapons, torsion artillery) plus refinements (pilum, gladius, carroballista); SOURCES.md names Rome 117 CE weapons ~3.3.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (iron cuirass, mail) exceeded: segmented plate and mail standard issue; well short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail.

ships.note: Anchor 3: triremes, liburnians, a few larger polyremes.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls, siege towers) plus permanent stone legionary fortresses and a fortified limes.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (engineered roads, depots) plus empire-wide granaries, annona shipping and river transport (part of anchor 4).

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores, speculatores, frontier watchtowers.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 (2011 int$) values for year 1 CE in Roman territory: Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt/Levant/Tunisia 1,116, France/Belgium/Portugal 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886. Mid ~1,000 is the rough population-weighted provincial average (Italy is ~1/8 of the population). Cross-check: Scheidel & Friesen 2009 (doi:10.3815/007543509789745223) put output at ~1.7-1.9x bare subsistence, consistent with this range.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994), ch. 3: army cost ~600-650 million HS a year in the 2nd century; GDP ~18 billion HS (Scheidel & Friesen 2009, doi:10.3815/007543509789745223: ~260 HS per head) -> ~3.5%.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess for an agrarian economy where ~75-85% of output was agricultural; mining, textiles, ceramics and construction make up the rest.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: GDP ~1.7-1.9x bare-bones subsistence (Scheidel & Friesen 2009) implies a modest surplus that fed ~15-20% urban population and the army.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks c. 200 CE; it reproduces arterial routes only, so the full engineered network was larger (high).

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites; ports able to supply a fleet or army (Ostia/Portus, Puteoli, Misenum, Ravenna, Alexandria, Carthage, Seleucia Pieria, Caesarea, Ephesus, Corinth, Massilia, Aquileia, Byzantium, Gades, Londinium...) estimated at ~20.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Rome alone imported ~200,000-300,000 t of grain a year; at ~2 voyages a season that needs ~100,000-150,000 t of shipping, and the annona was perhaps a quarter to a third of seaborne trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying their own grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; the Roman soldier carried ~3 days' rations plus mule-borne reserves.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.05-0.11 draft and pack animals (oxen, mules, donkeys, horses, camels) per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain and local supply plus fortified cities, the limes and broad population support; not 1.3 because the core is not protected by harsh climate.

notes: Snapshot = August 117 CE, at Trajan's death, the territorial peak. Population convention: everything inside the imperial border, slaves included; Armenia and Mesopotamia (annexed 114-116, abandoned by Hadrian in 118) are inside the border but their population is not counted in the mid. Border uses historical-basemaps world_100 (closest file), which shows the empire before the eastern annexations. Force numbers are Holder's c. 130 CE reconstruction (published unit lists, Hadrianic) applied to 117; the totals at Trajan's death were within a few percent (same number of legions). Navy numbers and ship counts are weak (no surviving order of battle). GDP per capita from the Maddison Project year-1 values for Roman provinces; all ancient GDP figures are reconstructions.
